lead: A laptop runs whatever program you install. An embedded system runs one program, fixed at manufacture, hidden inside a product with a job: a washing machine, a glucometer, a car's engine control unit. That single job decides the memory it may use, the power it may draw and the rupees it may cost. This chapter defines the term, lists the characteristics that follow, and maps the application areas.

sections.h3: A computer hidden inside a product

blocks.text: An embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to do one dedicated job. The computer is not the product: nobody buys a washing machine for its controller. Some syllabi call it a dedicated computer or a special-purpose computer.

The contrast is the general-purpose computer. On a laptop the user chooses the program. In an embedded system the program is firmware: machine code plus fixed data in ROM or flash, running from the instant power is switched on. The user cannot install another program; changing behaviour means flashing the chip. Memory choice for firmware is covered in 1.7.

The idea is old. The Apollo guidance computer of the 1960s flew a spacecraft on a fixed program held in about 36,000 words of read-only memory, with about 2,000 words of working memory. Today a ₹2,000 kitchen appliance carries a microcontroller with far more compute.

sections.h3: Characteristics that follow from one dedicated job

blocks.text: Fix the job and a chain of consequences follows. These are the properties an examiner means by the specialties of embedded systems.

items: Single function. One task, or a small fixed set of tasks, for the life of the product.
Tight hardware-software coupling. The code is written against one board, one memory map, one pin layout. Porting it means rewriting large parts.
Constrained resources. Memory counted in kilobytes, power in milliwatts, cost in rupees per unit, size in millimetres. Cost bites hardest, because the product ships in lakhs.
Reactive. It waits on inputs and answers them; it is not a batch job that runs to completion.
Often real-time. A deadline must be met. Real-time does not mean fast — it means a late answer is a wrong answer. An ABS controller must release brake pressure within milliseconds of a wheel locking.
Little or no user interface. A few LEDs, a seven-segment display, one button.
Firmware fixed at manufacture. Updates happen by flashing the chip, not by clicking install.
Long life and high reliability. An electricity meter runs for 15 years; a pacemaker must never need a reboot.

blocks.text: Not every system carries every property. A hobby board with a screen is embedded by function and general-purpose by interface. The list is a checklist, not a gate. How these properties are traded is the subject of 1.3.

Most embedded systems touch the physical world at two ends. At the input end sits a sensor: a device that converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal. The LM35 gives 10 mV for every 1 °C. An LDR drops its resistance when light falls on it. An IR sensor gives a voltage that says an object is in front of it. The input end may instead be a keypad, as on a washing machine, or a network link, as on a set-top box.

Signal conditioning stands between sensor and processor: amplify a millivolt signal to volts, filter noise, protect the pin from over-voltage. The processor then digitises the result with an ADC (Unit 3), runs the firmware, and decides.

At the output end sits an actuator: a device that converts an electrical signal into physical action — a DC motor turns, a relay contact closes, a solenoid valve opens, a buzzer sounds. A processor pin gives a few milliamps at 3.3 V; a motor wants hundreds of milliamps at 12 V. The driver is the switch in between: a transistor, a relay module, an H-bridge. Some systems drive only a display or a network link and no actuator, like a data logger.
The loop is sense, decide, act, repeat — thousands of times a second. Many systems also carry a network link so that the decision can be reported or corrected from outside (Unit 4).
The same sense-decide-act chain appears in every market. Read each row as input → process → output.

blocks.text: Three trends are reshaping this list. IoT puts every meter and appliance on a network. Edge AI runs a small model on the device instead of in the cloud. Low-power design aims at years of running from one coin cell. Where throughput is too high for a fixed processor, the logic moves into an FPGA instead (Unit 6). Choosing the processor is 1.5.

examples.question: Decide which of these are embedded systems and give input → process → output for each: (a) laptop, (b) IRCTC ATVM ticket machine, (c) washing machine, (d) digital electricity meter, (e) UPI soundbox.
steps: Test each device: is the computer inside a larger product, running fixed firmware for one job?
(a) Laptop: the user installs any software. General-purpose, not embedded.
(b) ATVM: card swipe and key presses → fare lookup → printed ticket. Embedded.
(c) Washing machine: water level and knob → wash-cycle program → motor and valve. Embedded.
(d) Electricity meter: sampled voltage and current → energy accumulation → LCD and pulse output. Embedded.
(e) UPI soundbox: payment message from the network → decode and verify → speaker announcement. Embedded.
Four embedded systems, one general-purpose computer.
examples.answer: Four of the five are embedded systems — ATVM, washing machine, electricity meter and UPI soundbox — and only the laptop is general-purpose.
examples.check:
devices = [('laptop', False), ('ATVM ticket machine', True), ('washing machine', True), ('digital electricity meter', True), ('UPI soundbox', True)]
embedded = sum(1 for name, is_emb in devices if is_emb)
general = len(devices) - embedded
print(embedded)
print(general)

traps: Small size does not make a system embedded. A laptop, or a Raspberry Pi running a desktop, is general-purpose however portable it is.
Real-time does not mean fast. A 1 ms deadline met on an 8-bit microcontroller is real-time; a fast server that misses its deadline is not.
'Embedded' is not another word for 'microcontroller'. The definition is about a dedicated function inside a product; the chip may be a microprocessor, a DSP, an SoC or an FPGA.
Sensor and actuator are opposites. An LM35 or LDR is a sensor; a buzzer, relay or solenoid valve is an actuator. Swapping them loses the whole mark.
The favourite definition question expects three elements: dedicated function, computer inside a larger product, and fixed firmware.

quiz.q: Define an embedded system in one sentence and name the two alternative terms some syllabi use.
quiz.a: A computer built inside a larger device, running fixed firmware for one dedicated job, usually under real-time, memory, power and cost limits. Alternatives: dedicated computer, special-purpose computer.

quiz.q: List any four characteristics of embedded systems.
quiz.a: Any four of: single function; tight hardware-software coupling; constrained memory, power, cost and size; reactive; real-time deadlines; little or no user interface; firmware fixed at manufacture; long life and high reliability.

quiz.q: Explain why a portable laptop is not an embedded system, even though it is small and light.
quiz.a: The user chooses the program and the hardware is built to run any software, so the function is not fixed. Size and portability are not the test; the test is a dedicated function with firmware fixed inside a larger product.

quiz.q: A UPI soundbox must announce a payment within 2 s of the message arriving. Decoding takes 250 ms and audio playback takes 1.2 s. What is the spare margin, in milliseconds?
quiz.a: Deadline = 2000 ms. Used = 250 + 1200 = 1450 ms. Margin = 2000 − 1450 = 550 ms. The margin is positive, so the deadline is met with 550 ms to spare.

quiz.q: Classify each as sensor or actuator: LM35, buzzer, LDR, relay, solenoid valve, IR sensor.
quiz.a: Sensors: LM35 (temperature), LDR (light), IR sensor (presence). Actuators: buzzer, relay, solenoid valve.

quiz.q: An electricity meter ships 1 million units a year. A designer proposes replacing a ₹150 8-bit microcontroller with a ₹900 Wi-Fi SoC to add remote reading. Analyse the trade-off.
quiz.a: Extra hardware cost is ₹900 − ₹150 = ₹750 per unit, so ₹750 × 1,000,000 = ₹75 crore a year. Gains: no manual reading, tamper alerts, live data. Costs: the Wi-Fi radio adds tens to hundreds of milliwatts of continuous draw and heat, which fights the meter's tight power budget and accuracy requirements; certification and firmware complexity rise; metering must keep working when the network is down. A common compromise keeps metering on the cheap part and adds a separate communication module.

beyond: Not for the exam. IoT puts every meter and appliance on a network, edge AI runs a small model on a microcontroller, and low-power design aims at a decade on one coin cell. Open instruction sets such as RISC-V are changing the cost of a custom microcontroller. Read a product datasheet and ask what its input chain, deadline and power budget are.
